title: High-severity routing approval policy
text: In this hypothetical company, P0 and P1 high-severity incidents require human approval before any AI-recommended team routing is applied. The assistant may suggest a team but must not perform routing changes.

title: Manual incident triage workload
text: In this fictional engineering scenario, repeated manual categorization and ticket routing are considered time-consuming. The company wants to test whether suggestions could reduce effort; no performance improvement has been measured.

title: Risk of incorrect incident classification
text: Incorrectly classifying or routing an incident may delay response. A safe pilot should include uncertainty flags, a manual fallback, and a method for engineers to correct suggestions.

title: Option A: rule-based triage
text: Rule-based incident classification uses explicit patterns and routing rules. It is easy to audit but may require maintenance when incident descriptions or team ownership change.

title: Option B: RAG-assisted classification
text: RAG-assisted incident categorization retrieves relevant runbooks and resolved ticket examples to ground an LLM suggestion. Retrieval quality and up-to-date documents remain important constraints.

title: Option C: agentic incident investigation
text: An agentic triage assistant could call read-only tools to inspect synthetic incident context and recommend a team. Tool permissions, latency, and human oversight need explicit limits.

title: New solutions and missing evidence
text: A newer incident automation approach may have fewer public studies. Missing evidence is not the same as negative evidence; compare required pilot tests and document uncertainty.

title: Data protection and tool restrictions
text: The hypothetical organization requires synthetic or approved public test data. Research tools must be read-only and must not expose credentials, private incident records, or customer details.
